Yesterday,  we celebrated a Torah Dedication honoring Hal Abroms’ Centennial year with friends and family! 

This Torah will travel to small cities all around Alabama bringing the Torah to Jewish families who may never have had a chance to see a Torah and connect to it. 

Hal grew up the small town of Dermott, Arkansas, and had little opportunity to connect to Jewish community and education as a child. With this special Torah, Jews is small communities will have the opportunity the connect to their heritage in a way that he never had growing up. 

Mazal Tov!

latestPosts.caption:
Mitzvot in Action! 

Our 7th and 8th graders had a special opportunity to put their Jewish learning into action by joining @chabadofalabama and helping with the mitzvah of building sukkot for families in our Birmingham Jewish community.

This experience was about so much more than building a sukkah. Our students experienced what it means to show up for others and strengthen our community through their own hands and hard work.

They also put two of our NEMJDS Middot into action: Community (Kehillah) and Leadership (Manhigut). Leadership isn’t always about being the person in charge—sometimes it means seeing what needs to be done, stepping forward, and helping make it happen.

We are so proud to see our students learning that mitzvot aren’t just something we study—they are something we do. 

Learning. Leading. Serving. Mitzvot in action.

latestPosts.caption:
What a beautiful and magnificent world we live in! From colorful flowers and breathtaking sunsets to the tiniest creatures 🐞 and the wonders of the human body, Hashem created it all!

Last week, we learned the very first story in the Torah: Baraishit, the story of how Hashem created the world and everything in it. We talked about how Hashem didn’t create the world in six days and then leave it on its own. He continues to recreate it every single moment! Knowing that Hashem is always in charge and caring for the world reminds us that we’re in good hands. 💛

To help us remember this important message, we made our very own Needohs! Give them a squeeze and remember: with Hashem in charge, we don’t have to worry! 🫧

We also played a fun game of bingo to review what Hashem created on each day. 

Check out all the fun we had! 😊

This past Sunday, we kicked off our exciting new JUDA curriculum: Bereishis – The Story of Our Lives! 📖✨

We explored the Torah as Hashem’s greatest gift, his words to guide us through life. We discovered the Chumash, its five books, which includes the stories of our Jewish family and the 613 mitzvot. We also learned how Torah teachings are so widely accessible today through many books, languages, apps, and websites so we can learn anytime, anywhere! 

This year, we’re traveling back to the very beginning to discover the stories of our first Jewish mothers and fathers, the roots of our Jewish family. 

To bring it all together, students built their very own edible Torah libraries!📚 A sweet reminder that Torah belongs to each of us and connects us to Hashem wherever we are. ❤️

🎥 Enjoy a peek at our first exciting JUDA lesson!

An Italian comedian did a bit about the contrast in talents of different cultural populations. Imagine going to the emergency room and Dr. Pallazzo comes out to see you, you call out, “got any Leibowitzes back there?” On the other hand, the Jews should get the Italians to cater the Seder, because after breakfast, Jewish cuisine has got nothing…

The cliché of the Jewish doctor! That being said…

This week I underwent a medical procedure. We checked in and I got into the gown and into bed. For a half hour or so, various nurses, techs, and other hospital staff approached to go through the preparatory steps required for the procedure. They were all very nice. As a certain point the doctor entered. He gave me a big smile and said Shalom. We chatted for a minute, and he was very up front about his Jewish identity (not that he could have hidden it from me…). This made me quite comfortable about a procedure that was less than thrilling.

While they were wheeling me to the procedure, the doctor looked in on Malkie in the waiting room and chatted with her. During their conversation, he pulled out his Mezuzah necklace and asked if it meant anything to her. To which she replied with a big smile, “it means Am Yisrael Chai” and then promptly invited him for Shabbos dinner.

During the procedure there were several people in the room. They were all wonderful and professional. I could not be more laudatory about my experience and that is credit to each of them and the role they played. For some reason, I felt a deeper connection with the doctor. At the time, with the sedation kicking in, I was unable to give it much thought. But as I recovered and reflected more on that, I realized that this was a feeling of brotherhood.

There are many good doctors. Contrary to the comedian’s assertion, they can be of any ethnicity. This was not only about the quality of the medical experience. This was about a soul connection. We are both Jewish and we have a shared history, destiny, and soul. 

The comforting feeling of brotherhood escorted me into la la land.

Y’all, the connection is real. We would do well to embrace it!

Shabbat Shalom
Rabbi Mendel Rivkin

latestPosts.caption:
For us, Sukkot is a holiday children can experience with their whole selves.

Our school stays open during the holiday, giving students time to eat in the sukkah, say the blessing, and make its traditions their own.

They assembled lulav sets, learning how the different parts fit together and what makes a set beautiful and kosher. Then came the sukkah-building competition. Each group built and decorated a sukkah and used it to tell the story of one of the ushpizin, the traditional guests of Sukkot. One sukkah featured a tiny David facing Goliath. Another had a bowl of lentil soup to tell Jacob’s story.

The children put so much thought and creativity into their work that choosing one winner felt impossible. Everyone got popcorn and a Jewish-themed video in place of a lesson. Their reaction when they heard the news was wonderful.

There was more: making chocolate treats, walking through the neighborhood, and visiting teachers’ sukkahs, where sweets were waiting for them. Our preschoolers visited the sukkah at the school’s new house, too.

This is how a holiday becomes part of a child’s life: through stories, food, building things together, and the joy of being there.

Some schools measure success by square footage.

We prefer report cards. 😉

The 2025–2026 school year has officially become the most successful in Shaloh House history.

🎓 100% acceptance to Boston Latin School — every single applicant got in (3 out of 3).

🥇 Three sixth graders earned Gold Medals at the International Math Olympiad, placing them in the top 2% of students worldwide.

✍️ And one of our students won 1st place in a nationwide essay competition, bringing a $25,000 award to Shaloh House.

Not bad for a school where everyone knows every child's name.

These achievements didn't happen because we teach to the test. They happened because curiosity is encouraged, questions are welcomed, hard work matters, and children are challenged to reach their full potential.

To our incredible students, dedicated teachers, supportive families, and everyone who makes Shaloh House what it is — thank you.

We're proud of what we've built together.

Today we mark Education and Sharing Day in Buffalo, commemorating 124 years since the birth of the Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem M. Schneerson — a global spiritual leader who championed the power of moral and ethical education to shape strong character and build a more united society.
The Rebbe taught that education is not only about knowledge, but about values — respect, kindness, responsibility, and service to others. His vision of a more peaceful and caring world continues to inspire acts of goodness and kindness, reminding us that even one positive action can create a ripple of change.

Education and Sharing Day is a meaningful opportunity to reflect on our shared responsibility to provide our youth with the tools and values they need to lead purposeful lives and strengthen our community.

We are grateful to Mayor Sean Ryan for recognizing Education and Sharing Day in Buffalo and for supporting initiatives that promote education, unity, and kindness throughout our city.

Let’s take a moment today to do something good — help a neighbor, show extra kindness, and invest in the next generation.

Because when we educate with values, we build a better future.

INTRODUCING: University of Oklahoma Chabad x Chai Vekayam ❤️🤍

Designed by OU students Alexis Novick, Elizabeth Ardizzone and Sophie Powell, this collection is a celebration of the warmth, connection, and sense of belonging they’ve found with Chabad.

For Jewish students at OU, Chabad becomes their true home away from home—a place to experience Joyful Judaism, friendship, and all the everyday moments that make college feel a little more like home.

18% of every website purchase goes directly back to the Jewish Sooners, helping support the programming and experiences that continue bringing students together.

Whether you’re proudly repping your Jewish identity across campus, or supporting the community that supports so many others, this collection was made to help you carry that feeling of belonging wherever you go.

University of Oklahoma Chabad x Chai Vekayam is available to shop on chaivekayam.org now.

Three years since October 7.

Three years of heartbreak. Three years of carrying the names, faces, stories, and memories of those we lost. Three years of watching incredible courage, sacrifice, resilience, and Jewish strength unfold before us.

Today, we remember the lives so brutally taken. We honor the soldiers, first responders, families, and ordinary people who showed extraordinary bravery. We hold our brothers and sisters in Israel close.

And we remember something deeply Jewish: when the world feels darker, our response is to add more light.

One more mitzvah.
One more act of kindness.
One more prayer.
One more moment of Torah.
One more person we reach out to.
One more way we choose to show up proudly and lovingly as Jews.

May every mitzvah we do today be in the merit of those who can no longer do one themselves, and may the memory of those we lost continue to inspire us to bring more goodness and light into the world.

We pray for healing, for strength, for peace, and for the day when we will be reunited with our loved ones with the coming of Moshiach.

Am Yisrael Chai. 💙
